inputs.text: Cannings jackpot model: each generation, with probability p_jackpot, one random individual survives and its offspring replace round(f x 2N) other gene copies; remaining copies reproduce deterministically.

inputs.name: 10% threshold
inputs.text: compression fails and a single family can replace more than ~10% of the population, the formula t̄ = 4Nₑ breaks in quantifiable ways. Below 10% replacement, the formula holds

inputs.name: P_fix = 1/(2N)
inputs.text: The fixation probability p = 1/(2N) is protected by the martingale property and holds exactly regardless of offspring distribution.

inputs.name: cross-checks outside the table
text: Day's large-N numbers reproduce: 1.363 and 1.737 at f = 0.5 (2N = 100, 800)
For a **fixed family** (m = 6) the excess shrinks: 1.0445 (2N = 60)
Exact f* (post hoc bisection) for +5% over the WF chain: 15% (2N = 20), 13% (30), 8% (50)

day.reading: above ~10% replacement t = 4Ne breaks (+15%, +21%, +29% over WF at 2N = 20/30/50); below it the formula holds; P_fix = 1/(2N)

critic.reading: the known multiple-merger result; P_fix unchanged; growth with N needs family size proportional to N, and a fixed family returns to the drift baseline

notes: All 27 table cells and the WF baseline reproduce to 0.00042; P_fix = i/2N to 1e-12 in every chain. The object's 14.9% and 28.8% are the column maxima over WF; its 20.4% uses the 2N = 30 cell at f = 50% (1.146), but that column peaks at f = 60% (1.148), giving 20.6% (gap 0.2 points; the claim file's derived line has the same slip, and the paper's ~21% holds). Over every integer m the exact peak excess over the exact WF chain is 15.0%, 20.7%, 28.8% (m/2N = 0.55, 0.57, 0.60). 'No deviation below about 10%' holds at the +5% cut for 2N = 20 and 30 (+3.9%, +4.9% at f = 10%) but not at 2N = 50 (+6.6%; f* = 8%). The table covers 2N = 20-50; in this chain f = 50% gives 1.363 at 2N = 100 (R4 E), while a fixed family of 6 falls from 1.0445 at 2N = 60 toward the drift baseline.
